graphic.headline: App launched to help Ghanaians verify prospective partners’ marital status before marriage
paragraphs: A new app designed to help people verify the marital status of their prospective partners before entering into marriage has been launched in Ghana.
Named Marrify, the app was launched in Accra on August 28, 2026, in partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MoGCSP).

The application operates as a searchable digital registry designed to bring transparency to marriage administration. It pulls legal data from the Registrar-General’s Department, courts, assemblies, and the Ghana Gazette.

The initiative is to help individuals carry out important checks before entering into a marriage and avoid the emotional, financial and legal complications that may arise when critical information about a prospective partner is not properly verified.

Beyond checking a prospective partner’s marital status, the Marrify app is a publicly searchable platform that enables the public to verify whether marriage venues, churches, pastors and Imams are duly licensed and registered to conduct marriages in Ghana.
The move is to promote greater transparency and accountability in marriage administration while helping prospective couples make more informed decisions before committing to marriage.

Speaking at the launch, the Minister of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, commended Marry Right Ghana for introducing an initiative aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and public confidence in marriage administration.
She emphasized that marriage extends beyond a legal union, highlighting its social, cultural and economic significance for individuals, children, families and communities.

ghanaweb.title: Marrify: What to know about Ghana’s new marriage verification platform
ghanaweb.headline: Marrify: What to know about Ghana’s new marriage verification platform
paragraphs:
Finding out that a person you are preparing to marry is already legally married can have serious emotional, financial and legal consequences.

A new digital platform launched in Ghana is seeking to make it easier for prospective couples to conduct checks on marital status before proceeding with marriage.

Known as Marrify, the platform was launched in Accra on August 28, 2026, in partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MoGCSP).

But what exactly is Marrify, what information can it provide, and what else can people check on the platform?

What is Marrify?

Marrify is a searchable digital registry designed to provide access to marriage-related information and support verification before marriage.

The platform draws legal data from sources including the Registrar-General's Department, courts, assemblies and the Ghana Gazette.

Its introduction is aimed at addressing situations where prospective spouses may not have access to important information about a partner's existing marital status.

Can you check if your partner is already married?

One of Marrify's key functions is the ability to verify the marital status of a prospective partner.

This means people preparing to enter into marriage can use the platform to conduct checks on whether information exists indicating that a prospective spouse has an existing marriage.

The development could be particularly relevant in situations where one party has not disclosed a previous or existing marriage to the person they intend to marry.

However, the availability and accuracy of any result will depend on the records contained in the official sources connected to the system.

What else can you check on Marrify?

Marrify is not limited to checking prospective spouses.

The platform also allows members of the public to verify whether marriage venues, churches, pastors and Imams are duly licensed and registered to conduct marriages in Ghana.

This gives prospective couples an opportunity to look beyond the person they intend to marry and also establish whether the individuals and institutions involved in conducting their marriage have the required registration or licensing.

Why does marital-status verification matter?

Marriage involves more than the wedding ceremony itself.

Where a person enters a marriage without knowing that their prospective spouse has an existing marriage, the consequences can extend beyond emotional distress.

There may also be legal and financial complications, particularly where questions arise about the validity of a subsequent marriage or obligations arising from an existing union.

The introduction of Marrify is therefore intended to make relevant information more accessible and encourage people to conduct appropriate checks before marriage.

What the Gender Minister said

At the launch, the Minister of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, said marriage has social, cultural and economic significance beyond its status as a legal union.

She commended Marry Right Ghana for introducing the initiative, saying it could strengthen transparency, accountability and public confidence in marriage administration.

According to her, tools such as Marrify have the potential to protect prospective couples from entering unions based on incomplete or false information.

She further noted that undisclosed information could contribute to disputes, fraud and emotional harm.

ghanamma_launch.title: Ghana Launches Digital Platform To Verify Marriage, Divorce Records – Ghanamma.com
ghanamma_launch.headline: Ghana Launches Digital Platform To Verify Marriage, Divorce Records
paragraphs: Ghana has introduced a digital platform that enables members of the public to verify marriage and divorce records, as well as confirm the status of marriage officers, licensed venues and Imams, YEN reports on Friday.
The platform, called Marrify, was unveiled in Accra on August 28 by Marry Right Ghana Limited in collaboration with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection.
Marrify functions as an online marriage and divorce registry, providing access to records covering ordinance, customary and Islamic marriages.
Members of the public can conduct searches using information such as the names of individuals, spouses’ names, towns, churches, denominations, certificate numbers and Gazette numbers.

Beyond marriage records, the platform features a database of marriage officers authorised to conduct civil or ordinance marriages. Users can also verify licensed marriage venues and Imams through the platform.

According to the platform, its database is compiled from records obtained from institutions including the Registrar-General’s Department, courts, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, as well as the Ghana Gazette.

Speaking at the launch, the Minister of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, urged prospective couples to carry out proper checks on their partners, proposed marriage venues and officiating persons before proceeding with their unions.
She said, “It is a reminder of the need to uphold the highest standard of integrity and accountability.

“You would not have to take a person’s word for it, even in the most trusted relationship. You can verify with this app. And then again, when making a decision on the venue, who has to officiate the marriage, where it is officiated, the officiant, and the status of the one you are getting married to.

“These are the critical issues we need to ponder over, verify and be sure of before taking the needed step. As a ministry, we’ve used our platform to promote the app and engage with our stakeholders and potential beneficiaries. To ensure that Ghanaians live in awareness. So that you do not invest for so many years, resources and find out that all the investment has gone in vain.”

Lartey further called on Marry Right Ghana to collaborate with government agencies, religious organisations, traditional institutions and other relevant stakeholders to maintain the accuracy of information on the platform and ensure that records are updated regularly.
The digital registry also includes divorce records arising from court rulings and judgments, with some divorce entries linked to the corresponding marriage records.

However, Marrify warns users that its database is still being populated. It therefore advises that the absence of a record in a search should not, on its own, be regarded as confirmation that an individual has never been married.
The platform also provides a mechanism for individuals and institutions to submit marriage and divorce records, alongside relevant supporting documents, for verification.

ghanamma_rollout.title: Ghana rolls out Marrify to simplify marital-status checks – Ghanamma.com
ghanamma_rollout.headline: Ghana rolls out Marrify to simplify marital-status checks
paragraphs: Ghanaian marriage and divorce records can now be searched through a single digital platform. Called Marrify, the solution was recently launched in Accra by Marry Right Ghana Ltd in partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection. It allows users to search registered marriage and divorce records and verify authorized marriage officers, approved venues, churches and imams.

Marrify operates as a searchable digital registry drawing on multiple sources. The platform says it uses data from the Registrar General’s Department, courts, local assemblies and the Ghana Gazette. Searches can be conducted using a person’s name, a spouse’s name, a locality, a church, a certificate number or a Gazette reference.
The initiative aims to help users access information that was previously spread across different administrative channels.

The centralization comes as Ghana continues to operate several marriage registration regimes. The country distinguishes between ordinance marriages, customary marriages and Muslim marriages, each of which follows different registration procedures.

For an ordinance marriage, the Registrar General’s Department requires a notice to be filed with the registrar, followed by a publication period before a certificate can be issued if no objection is raised. Customary marriages, meanwhile, are registered with the relevant local authorities.

Putting marriage records online does not mean that all marital information in Ghana is already available. Marrify says records are still being added progressively and warns that an unsuccessful search does not necessarily mean that a certificate does not exist.
The platform also plans to link records to the relevant institutions, officers and venues to make verification easier.

Data coverage is therefore one of the initiative’s main challenges. At the launch, Minister of Gender Agnes Naa Momo Lartey said the platform’s effectiveness would depend on public confidence in the information it provides and on cooperation from institutions responsible for registering marriages.
Marrify also offers tools for government agencies, courts and religious organizations, alongside an artificial intelligence assistant focused on Ghanaian matrimonial law.

itweb.title: Ghana launches digital marriage records platform | ITWeb Africa
itweb.headline: Ghana launches digital marriage records platform
itweb.author: Samuel Olomu
paragraphs: Ghana has launched Marrify, a digital platform that allows users to search and verify registered marriage and divorce records.

Launched in Accra on 28 August by Marry Right Ghana Ltd in partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Marrify also allows users to verify marriage officers, licensed venues, churches, pastors and imams.

The platform draws legal data from the Registrar-General's Department, courts, assemblies and the Ghana Gazette, creating a searchable digital registry intended to improve transparency and access to marriage information.
The platform also provides tools for government agencies, churches and courts, alongside an artificial intelligence assistant providing information on Ghanaian marriage law.
Marrify comes as Ghana's marriage-registration system continues to rely on formal processes involving registrars and licensed marriage officers.

The Registrar-General's Department requires couples seeking marriage under the ordinance to give notice to the marriage registrar and complete the prescribed documentation before the marriage is solemnised.

The department says its mission includes providing efficient administration, customer-friendly services and accurate data, while Marrify aims to make registered information more accessible outside registry offices.

However, the platform's usefulness depends on the completeness and accuracy of the records available to it. Ghana recognises different forms of marriage, including ordinance, customary and Islamic marriages, which are subject to different registration arrangements.
This means an absence of a record in Marrify should not necessarily be interpreted as proof that a person has never been married.
Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, minister for gender, children and social protection, said the initiative addresses the need for reliable information before people enter into marriage.

“The effectiveness of such a platform will ultimately depend on public confidence in the information it provides and the cooperation of institutions responsible for marriage registration,” said Lartey.
The comment points to a broader challenge for Marrify: maintaining accurate and complete records as information is consolidated from government registries, courts and local authorities.
Marrify's longer-term value will therefore depend not only on its search technology but also on the quality, coverage and regular updating of the records underpinning the platform.

technext.title: Ghana launches Marrify to make marriage and divorce records searchable online
technext.headline: Ghana launches Marrify to make marriage and divorce records searchable online
paragraphs: Ghana is moving marriage verification from public notices and scattered records to digital searches with Marrify, a newly launched platform that makes marriage-related information available online.

The platform, launched in Accra on August 28 in partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, allows users to search marriage and divorce records as well as verify marriage officers, venues and licensed Imams.

While Marrify has been presented as a tool for prospective couples to check the marital status of their partners, its wider offering reflects a shift in how marriage-related information can be accessed and verified.

Before now, marriage registration and verification involved records held across different institutions and processes, including the Registrar-General’s Department, courts, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies and the Ghana Gazette.
Marriage registration processes have also relied on public notices, with information published to allow objections before some marriages are registered or solemnised.
Marrify is seeking to bring parts of these records and verification processes into a searchable digital platform.

The platform says its database includes Gazette records dating from 1886 to 2026 and links records across customary, Islamic and ordinance marriages. It also connects divorce and annulment records to the original marriage records where available.

Users searching the platform can open records to view information including their source, dates, issuing authority and relevant licence context.

Beyond individual marriage records, Marrify provides searchable information on ministers of religion gazetted to solemnise ordinance marriages, licensed marriage venues and Islamic marriage authorities.
Its venue database can be searched by town, assembly, denomination and region, while a denomination section links marriage venues, officers and records associated with church bodies.

The platform also claims to cover all 16 regional coordinating councils and 261 Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, while tracking three licence categories covering venues, marriage officers and Imams.

Marrify’s model goes beyond making historical records available for public searches. The platform has separate portals for MMDAs, churches, the Registrar-General’s Department and courts, allowing institutions to submit or manage records. It also provides a self-reporting and record-claim process for individuals and institutions seeking to add or claim missing information.
For Ghanaians living abroad, Marrify also says its searchable records can support verification needs involving embassies, courts and personal documentation.

The platform includes a timeline of Ghana’s marriage laws and administration, tracing developments from the 1884 Marriage Ordinance and the beginning of Gazette records in 1886 through subsequent legislation governing Islamic, customary and other forms of marriage.
Marrify also features a Family Law AI assistant, which it says can provide support for family-law research, drafting and document review.

The platform is operated by Marry Right Ghana and describes itself as a “National Marriage & Divorce Registry”, with a stated focus on digitisation, verification and public access to marriage-related records.
